findings.title: `394` columns hold raw intensities, and total signal differs by sample.
findings.detail: `394` columns run from `11.1` to `4,540,897`, unlogged. Each sample's total signal runs from `23,652,064` to `37,670,677`, a 1.6-fold spread that dilution alone can make.
findings.why_it_matters: A more dilute sample has smaller values in every feature, so a model fit to raw intensities can read dilution as biology, and the raw scale lets a few abundant features dominate. Linear models wait until a normalization is chosen or you state the values are already normalized.
findings.summary: `394` columns are raw intensities; total signal varies 1.6-fold, so dilution would read as biology.

repairs.sentence: Of the 394 intensity columns, those of them the models take as exposures were normalized by probabilistic quotient normalization (Dieterle et al. 2006), the reference spectrum the median of the integral-normalized training rows within each fold, then log2-transformed.

findings.title: Your missing values cluster in the lowest-abundance features.
findings.detail: Across 396 features, a feature's missing rate tracks its abundance rank at a rank correlation of -0.97. 307 features have blanks; the highest rate is 55%, on one of the least abundant.
findings.why_it_matters: In metabolomics that usually means below the detection limit — left-censored rather than missing at random — and filling with a median would place non-detections in the middle of the distribution. Half the minimum observed is the convention, and it is the one a reader can check.
findings.summary: Missing values cluster in the lowest-abundance features: likely below detection, not missing at random.

findings.title: There is a run-order column, and intensity tracks it.
findings.detail: `run_order` runs 1 to 80 with every position used exactly once. 253 of 394 features (64%) have a Spearman correlation with it beyond 0.3 that survives Benjamini–Hochberg at 5%. With no drift, about 1% of features would pass |ρ| > 0.3 by chance at 80 injections (here 64% do), and almost none would also survive the correction.
findings.why_it_matters: Instrument drift is often the largest single variance component in a metabolomics run, larger than the biology. Correction is not applied here: it alters every value in the table, so it is a decision rather than a default.
findings.summary: Intensity tracks `run_order` in `64%` of features: the signal drifts over the run. No control for this yet.

findings.title: 8 of 80 rows are instrument runs, not biological samples.
findings.detail: Reading the sample names and the run-type columns (`sample_id`, `sample_type`) against the field's naming conventions: 8 pooled QC (`sample_id` matches `^QC`, e.g. 'QC01'). That leaves 72 biological samples.
findings.why_it_matters: Quality-control, blank, standard and system-suitability injections are the instrument being checked, not people being measured. They belong in the quality assessment and out of the modeling rows, and the reading here is the naming convention rather than the values — so it is worth confirming against your run list.

findings.title: `394` columns hold raw intensities, and total signal differs by sample.
findings.detail: `394` columns run from `11.1` to `4,540,897`, unlogged. Each sample's total signal runs from `23,652,064` to `37,670,677`, a 1.6-fold spread that dilution alone can make.
findings.why_it_matters: A more dilute sample has smaller values in every feature, so a model fit to raw intensities can read dilution as biology, and the raw scale lets a few abundant features dominate. Linear models wait until a normalization is chosen or you state the values are already normalized.

findings.title: Your missing values cluster in the lowest-abundance features.
findings.detail: Across 396 features, a feature's missing rate tracks its abundance rank at a rank correlation of -0.97. 307 features have blanks; the highest rate is 55%, on one of the least abundant.
findings.why_it_matters: In metabolomics that usually means below the detection limit — left-censored rather than missing at random — and filling with a median would place non-detections in the middle of the distribution. Half the minimum observed is the convention, and it is the one a reader can check.
findings.summary: Missing values cluster in the lowest-abundance features: likely below detection, not missing at random.

findings.title: There is a run-order column, and intensity tracks it.
findings.detail: `run_order` runs 1 to 80 with every position used exactly once. 253 of 394 features (64%) have a Spearman correlation with it beyond 0.3 that survives Benjamini–Hochberg at 5%. With no drift, about 1% of features would pass |ρ| > 0.3 by chance at 80 injections (here 64% do), and almost none would also survive the correction.
findings.why_it_matters: Instrument drift is often the largest single variance component in a metabolomics run, larger than the biology. Correction is not applied here: it alters every value in the table, so it is a decision rather than a default.
findings.summary: Intensity tracks `run_order` in `64%` of features: the signal drifts over the run. No control for this yet.

findings.title: 8 of 80 rows are instrument runs, not biological samples.
findings.detail: Reading the sample names and the run-type columns (`sample_id`, `sample_type`) against the field's naming conventions: 8 pooled QC (`sample_id` matches `^QC`, e.g. 'QC01'). That leaves 72 biological samples.
findings.why_it_matters: Quality-control, blank, standard and system-suitability injections are the instrument being checked, not people being measured. They belong in the quality assessment and out of the modeling rows, and the reading here is the naming convention rather than the values — so it is worth confirming against your run list.

versus_baseline.tolerance_basis: Better only when the gain's 95% interval lies above zero and the gain is at least 0.01 (a convention): a gain above 0.073. The interval is corrected for the 50 folds sharing training rows (Nadeau & Bengio 2003).

calibration.smoother: lowess, span 2/3, no robustness iterations (as rms val.prob)

models.performance: Cross-validated log loss 0.692 (95% interval 0.685 to 0.699, likely too narrow (Bates, Hastie & Tibshirani 2023): 395 candidate predictors for 57 rows (p/n 6.9, above the 1 this app takes as p ≫ n)) by 5-fold cross-validation: the expected performance of this modeling procedure at this sample size.
models.methods: Within each training fold, PQN, detection-limit-aware imputation, log transformation and autoscaling were fitted and applied to the held-out fold; elastic-net parameters were tuned in an inner CV nested in an outer CV. Values below detection in 306 features were filled after normalization and before the log, each by its expected value below the limit under a left-censored normal fitted to the feature's logarithm on the training fold (Lubin et al. 2004).

base.cv_definition: Cross-validated scores are the mean over folds; the fold values show the spread.
base.se_definition: Each standard error counts which rows were scored, with each fold's model as fitted (LeDell et al. 2015; DeLong's for the AUC); it leaves out how the models would vary with other training rows.
base.precision: On these 57 training rows the cross-validated log loss has a standard error of 0.004 for Elastic net; whether two families differ is read from their paired interval, not from either one alone.
base.imbalance: The event, `1`, is 46% of the training rows. No resampling (SMOTE, over- or undersampling) or class weighting was applied: customary in machine-learning papers, resampling overestimates the rarer class's probability without raising the AUC (van den Goorbergh et al. 2022); a decision moves the threshold instead.
base.tension: AUC is the customary headline: it ranks risks without asking whether they are right (semi-proper), so the models were compared, chosen and declared on log loss, a strictly proper score (Van Calster et al., STRATOS TG6).

comparison.method: the corrected repeated k-fold t (Nadeau & Bengio 2003; Bouckaert & Frank 2004)
